questions.question: How does npm's dependency model work — package.json, the semver ranges, lockfiles, and dependency types?
questions.title: Npm Dependency Model
questions.direct_answer: package.json is the manifest (name/version/scripts/deps); package-lock.json is the EXACT resolved tree (every package at an exact version — reproducible installs; commit it). Dependency types: dependencies (runtime — ships in the bundle), devDependencies (build/test only — never installed for consumers of your library), peerDependencies ('I need my CONSUMER to provide this' — the plugin/version-compat mechanism; npm 7+ auto-installs peers), optionalDependencies (failures tolerated). Semver ranges: ^1.2.3 (compatible: 1.x.x — minor+patch updates allowed), ~1.2.3 (patch only), exact 1.2.3, and the x-ranges — npm install saves ^ by default (the 'why did 1.3 break me' answer). The tree model: node_modules is NESTED (each package gets its own copies where version conflicts demand it — the deduped flat root where possible); multiple versions CAN coexist (different subtrees), unlike the single-version assumptions of some other ecosystems.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The moving parts, verified:

```bash
npm install express              # adds to dependencies with ^range
npm install -D vitest            # devDependencies — build/test only
npm ci                           # CLEAN install EXACTLY from the lockfile
                                 # (CI/production — never 'install' there)
npm outdated                     # what's behind its range
npm ls left-pad                  # WHY is this in my tree (the path)
npm dedupe                      # flatten duplicate versions where compatible

npm publish                      # ships 'files' + package.json
npx playwright install          # run without installing globally
```

Semver ranges (the resolution rules):
```text
^1.2.3  → >=1.2.3 <2.0.0   (minor+patch allowed — the npm default)
~1.2.3  → >=1.2.3 <1.3.0   (patch only)
1.2.3   → exactly          (the lockfile uses exact versions)
^0.x.y   → careful: 0.x treats x like a major (breaking allowed in 0.x)
```
The semver CONTRACT: MAJOR = breaking, MINOR = feature (backwards-compatible), PATCH = fix — and the trust problem: a dependency CAN break you without touching major (the reason lockfiles + npm ci exist: the lockfile pins the RESOLVED tree; 'npm install' inside a project honors the lock unless ranges drifted — but fresh installs without a lock resolve today's latest).

The dependency TYPES (each answers a different question): dependencies = 'my code imports this at RUNTIME' (bundled/shipped); devDependencies = 'my workflow needs this' (test runners, linters, bundlers — excluded for library CONSUMERS installing my package); peerDependencies = 'I integrate with the consumer's copy of this' (a React component package peer-depends on react — the consumer's React, not a nested one: singletons like React, plugins, and CSS-in-JS libraries are the classic cases — the version RANGE communicates compat: ^18); optionalDependencies = install if possible, skip silently (platform-specific binaries). engines (the node version constraint — warns, doesn't block unless engine-strict) and workspaces (the monorepo protocol: one root lockfile for all packages).

The lifecycle scripts (the hooks that build the ecosystem): prepare (runs on pack AND on consumer install — the transpile-on-install pattern for src-only packages), preinstall/postinstall (native builds — node-gyp, playwright's browser download), prepublishOnly (the publish gate: run tests before shipping). The security layer: npm audit (known-CVE matching against the tree), npm overrides (force a transitive version — the quarantine tool while waiting for upstream), and npm ls + why to trace who pulls what.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    MAN[package.json manifest] --> LOCK[package-lock.json exact resolved tree — COMMIT IT]
    DEP[dependencies] --> RUN[runtime — ships]
    DEV[devDependencies] --> BUILD[build/test only — not for consumers]
    PEER[peerDependencies] --> CONSUMER[consumer provides — singletons, plugins]
    OPT[optionalDependencies] --> TOLERANT[failures tolerated]
    R1['^1.2.3'] --> MINOR['>=1.2.3 <2.0.0 — npm default']
    R2['~1.2.3'] --> PATCH['<1.3.0']
    R3['1.2.3'] --> EXACT['lockfile form']
    TREE[node_modules nested + deduped flat root] --> MULTI[conflicting versions can coexist in subtrees]
    CI['npm ci'] --> REPRODUCIBLE[exact lockfile install — CI and prod]
    AUDIT['npm audit / overrides'] --> SEC[known-CVE scan, transitive quarantine]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The install algorithm (why the tree looks like it does): npm resolves the ROOT manifest's ranges → builds a virtual tree satisfying every constraint → where two packages need incompatible versions of X, X is NESTED under one of them (node_modules is a nesting, not a flat list — with hoisting to the root where versions coincide). The lockfile records the RESOLVED shape — both so installs are reproducible AND so the dedupe decisions don't drift between machines. That's also why phantom dependencies work-but-shouldn't: hoisted packages land in the ROOT node_modules and your code can require them WITHOUT declaring them (works locally, breaks for consumers or after dedup shuffles — the pnpm hard-isolation model exists to kill this class).

The publish/consume contract (the library side): 'files' (or .npmignore) controls what ships; main/module/exports (the exports map is the modern form — subpath permissions and encapsulation: 'import x from "pkg/sub"' only works if exported, ending the deep-import hazard); types field for TS resolution; and the dual-package hazard (CJS + ESM both shipped — an ESM-import of the CJS copy or vice versa creates TWO instances of a singleton (the instanceof-fails bug) — the 'default' interop and the migration-era 'ESM wrapper' patterns exist to keep ONE instance).

The ecosystem alternatives (the comparison layer): yarn (the drop-in with workspaces-first ergonomics), pnpm (the content-addressed store + symlinked node_modules — strict, fast, no phantom deps: the monorepo favorite), and Bun (the runtime+package-manager combo — install speed as headline). The registry protocol stays shared (npmjs.org; scoped @org/pkg; private registries via .npmrc). The workflow advice that survives any manager: commit the lockfile, npm ci (or equivalent) in CI, engines pinned in the manifest, and updates as DELIBERATE PRs (renovate/dependabot) rather than drift.
